legend: CK5 immunostaining demonstrates myoepithelial cells surrounding intermediate-grade ductal carcinoma in situ on the left and normal acini of a lobule on the right, but staining is absent around microinvasive carcinoma in the central part. Note the lymphoid reaction.

diagnosis: Ductal carcinoma in situ spreading to sclerosing adenosis
legend: This is a frequent mimic of microinvasion. At low power, the distorted but maintained lobular architecture can be appreciated.

diagnosis: Ductal carcinoma in situ spreading to sclerosing adenosis
legend: This is a frequent mimic of microinvasion. At medium power, the small acini involved are suggestive of microinvasion, with the haphazardly oriented tumour cell nests.

diagnosis: Ductal carcinoma in situ spreading to sclerosing adenosis
legend: This is a frequent mimic of microinvasion. Immunostaining for calponin (a cytoplasmic myoepithelial marker) reveals attenuated myoepithelium around all tumour cell clusters and nests.
The central area shows an invasive lobular carcinoma < 1 mm with oedematous stromal reaction; this is surrounded by lobular neoplasia (lobular carcinoma in situ).
Sclerosing adenosis adjacent to low-grade cribriform ductal carcinoma in situ and papilloma, mimicking invasion.
The presence of myoepithelial cells is clearly highlighted with dual immunostaining for cytokeratin (red) and p63 (brown).

diagnosis: Microinvasive carcinoma associated with high-grade ductal carcinoma in situ
legend: High-grade ductal carcinoma, which is identified as microinvasive carcinoma arising from high-grade ductal carcinoma in situ by dual immunostaining for cytokeratin and p63 (shown in <<#5237>>Fig. 2.XXX).

diagnosis: Microinvasive carcinoma associated with high-grade ductal carcinoma in situ
legend: High-grade ductal carcinoma, which is identified as microinvasive carcinoma arising from high-grade ductal carcinoma in situ by dual immunostaining for cytokeratin (red) and p63 (brown).

A case of high-grade ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) with scant foci of microinvasion in the adjacent tissue (< 1 mm to the margin of DCIS). The presence of single-cell infiltration as seen in this case (in the top left of the field) supports the diagnosis of microinvasion.
High grade DCIS shows necrosis, calcifications and lymphocytic infiltrates. Microinvasion (arrow) is present. Haemorrhage and cavitation from previous biopsy are seen.
